pr.title: Bound the site workflow's API calls, and finish the installer's rollout
pr.head: e369424a72abbc17a354a55ad0c165ec83db7e7c

summary: multipass's website, getmultipass.dev, holds one page and a few redirects. Its main job is to send curl -fsSL https://getmultipass.dev/install.sh | bash to the installer attached to a GitHub release. The Website workflow, .github/workflows/site.yml, deploys the site to Vercel on each merge to main. It then moves the domain to the new deployment through Vercel's REST API and checks the live redirects. When a check fails, it rolls the domain back to the deployment it served before.
This pull request does two things:

1. It hardens that workflow. It takes the three suggestions the review of #38 left: a time limit on every Vercel API call, a format check on every deployment ID the workflow reads back from Vercel, and a fix for a Cache-Control check that passed its test only by crashing under macOS's old bash.
  2. It finishes the installer project. The README's Install section now leads with the one-line install, and the installer plan is marked completed, with a new § 9 that records what shipped and the evidence for it.

The workflow changes run only on main with the Vercel token, so the next Website run is the first to exercise them. This head also merges main, which brought in the password generator, and resolves one conflict in the README's trust paragraph. The resolution keeps main's new line counts and this pull request's install bullets. The Projector review has one open finding, on the README's one-line install, and one suggestion and one follow-up. Each appears as a note on the line it concerns.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Deployment: one upload of site/ to Vercel. Its ID looks like dpl_….
  • Alias: the record saying which deployment the domain serves. GET /v4/aliases/getmultipass.dev returns it as deploymentId.
  • Promote: point the domain at a new deployment. Rollback points it back at the one recorded before.
  • $GITHUB_OUTPUT: the file a step writes name=value lines to, which later steps read. A newline inside a value would start a second line, so a value from outside must not hold one.
  • Attestation: GitHub's signed record of which workflow built a file, which gh attestation verify checks.

groups.title: Bounded, checked calls to Vercel
groups.kicker: A time limit on each API call, and a format check on each deployment ID
intro: Every call the workflow makes to Vercel's API goes through vercel-api.sh. It sends the token to curl on stdin, so the token never appears in a process's arguments. Before this change, curl had no time limit. A request that never answered could hold the job, and the site concurrency group that blocks the next deploy, for up to GitHub's six-hour job limit. Each request now ends after 30 seconds and counts as a failure.

The workflow also reads two deployment IDs back from Vercel: the one the domain serves before the deploy, which is the rollback target, and the new one. Both go into $GITHUB_OUTPUT and into later API paths. Each must now match ^dpl_[A-Za-z0-9]+$, or its step fails with a message naming the value. An empty ID before the deploy still means there is nothing to roll back to.

checks.text: A failed or timed-out call still fails its step, and a failed promotion still triggers the rollback. This was traced through each step: curl exits 28 on a timeout, vercel-api.sh then exits 1, and the rollback step's condition includes steps.promote.outcome == 'failure'.

files.note: Adds --max-time 30 to every request. The token still reaches curl only through -H @-.

checks.text: With 30 seconds per request, one 36-try alias wait (five seconds apart) can last about 21 minutes in the worst case, rather than three. That is still far short of the six-hour job limit.

files.note: Checks the alias's deployment ID and the new deployment's ID against ^dpl_[A-Za-z0-9]+$ before writing either to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.

checks.text: The pattern matches the whole value. Running it on hostile inputs rejected an ID followed by a newline and deployment=evil, an ID with /../ or ?, a leading or trailing space, dpl_, and the multi-line output jq -r gives for an array.

Suggestion from the review: a 2xx answer whose deploymentId is missing or null still records no rollback target, just as a 404 does. Requiring an ID on any 2xx would keep a failed promotion from staying live in that case.
The new deployment's ID must now match the pattern, which also covers an empty ID, so this one check replaces the old -z test.

files.note: cache_revalidates refuses an empty Cache-Control value before it splits the value into directives.

checks.text: Under macOS's /bin/bash 3.2, check-site.sh cache refuses "", " ", ",", ",," and "public," with exit 1 and no output. Before this change, an empty value crashed with directives[@]: unbound variable.
Follow-up from the review: the live check's curl has no --max-time. A response that never finishes keeps the new deployment live, with its rollback still waiting, until the job's six-hour limit.

files.note: Adds a " " case, and fails a refusal that prints anything, so a crash no longer counts as a refusal.

checks.text: With main's check-site.sh, this test prints FAIL: … failed on "" without applying the rule for "" and " ". With this branch it ends with site checks passed. Both runs used /bin/bash 3.2.

groups.title: The installer's rollout, finished
groups.kicker: The README leads with the one-line install, and the plan records the outcome
intro: The installer project's last rollout step was to point the README at the one-line install once the release and the domain checked out. The first automatic Website run after #38 deployed, promoted and passed the live check, so this pull request takes that step and marks the plan completed.

The README now explains each way to install and what it trusts: a build from source, the attested prebuilt binary, and the one-liner through getmultipass.dev. It also gives GitHub's own URL, a pinned release, a check-first install that verifies install.sh before running it, and install.sh verify, which rebuilds a release and compares the bytes.

checks.text: One planned DNS record is left out on purpose. Rollout step 6 was to add 0 issuewild ";", but Vercel also issues a wildcard certificate for its default * record, which cannot be removed, and the record would stop that certificate renewing. § 2.9, step 6 and § 6.1 all say so.

files.note: Rewrites the trust paragraph and the Install section around the one-line install.

checks.text: Each claim was checked against install.sh and release.yml. Rust selects the source build, and the prebuilt binary is for macOS only. Without gh the installer stops unless MULTIPASS_UNVERIFIED=1 is set, and MULTIPASS_VERSION pins a release. status, uninstall and verify <version> work after bash -s --. The release attests install.sh in multipass.sigstore.json, which the check-first command verifies.

Open review finding: this command installs the newest release, v0.1.0. That release has only init, list, passwd, add, get, rm, otp and upgrade, and keeps a single-file store.age. The rest of the README describes the store package, Touch ID unlock, rekey, history and generate, which a reader who installs this way does not get. The fix is to say so in the Install section, or to wait for 0.2.0 before leading with the one-liner.

files.note: Marks the plan completed, records the first automatic site run and the issuewild decision, and adds § 9 Outcome.

checks.text: § 9 lists, for each check in § 4, its evidence, or why it has not run yet: the checks that need a second release, the rollback, which needs a bad deployment, and verify against v0.1.0, which needs a Mac with the release's SDK.
